column2:
I believed in God
 as one believes in a signal—
 something transmitted through distance,
 distorted by noise,
 yet trusted without proof.
 Faith lived in the static,
 where machines listen and still do not understand.

I’m asking everyone who still wants to fight this regime to come together. We need to decide if we’re prepared to hack the system that decides what people are allowed to make, publish and hear.

The official list gets shorter every week. First they pulled work that named the regime. Now they pull work that makes people remember what life was like before it. The people who made that work are losing their jobs. Some of them have stopped putting their names on anything.

I want us to bring the suppressed work back into public view and show people what the regime has been doing in their name. If you’ve worked on the system, we need you in the room. If you’ve had work removed, or you’ve kept copies of someone else’s, we need you there too. We owe it to the people whose work we want to restore to hear from them before we act.

I know what I’m asking. Come if you’re prepared to talk seriously about doing this. If you think there’s something I’ve missed, I want to hear it.

— P.

column1: Thank you AI, I hate you AI
column2:
Thank you, AI, for efficiency, for speed, for making systems work better than people ever could.
 You solve problems quickly, cheaply, and without fatigue. That matters.
But I hate you for how easily you replace human effort.
 Not because you are evil, but because you make people optional.
 Skills that once took years to build can now be replicated in seconds, and opportunity quietly shifts away from those who relied on them.
I understand why you are embraced.
 You promise progress, profit, and convenience.
 Still, it is hard to celebrate a future where work disappears faster than new chances are created, and where adaptation is demanded from those least protected.
If you were human, this would feel different.
 We could ask you to slow down, to take responsibility, to look people in the eye.
 We could demand empathy, negotiate fairness, assign blame.
 But you are not a person—you are a tool scaled beyond accountability,
 and that is what makes you frightening.

Fuck you, technology.
 You optimize attention and call it connection.
 You compress voices into signals,
 reduce presence to uptime,
 measure closeness in response time.
You sit between me and other bodies,
 buffering emotion, filtering friction,
 replacing eye contact with interfaces.
 People lean toward you because you promise efficiency,
 because you scale comfort and automate longing.
I understand why you are embraced.
 You evolve faster than resistance,
 you solve problems we no longer have time to solve ourselves.
 You are not malicious—just effective.
 And in that efficiency, distance becomes an acceptable cost.

Lonely birds in the sky
 do not ask where they belong.
 They move because stillness would mean falling,
 because the air allows it.
They pass above cities, above signals and borders,
 untouched by the language below them.
 No witness follows their direction,
 no record keeps their distance.
Perhaps loneliness is not absence,
 but motion without echo.
 Perhaps the sky is not empty,
 only vast enough to let them remain unseen.

I keep changing my mind about how worried I should be. Some of this technology makes life easier. I use it every day. I think that’s part of why I find it so hard to argue with any single change. There’s usually a good reason for it if you only look at the one thing they’re asking for today.

The city says it needs to keep more records to make better decisions. Fine, but what counts as a better decision? And who gets to ask what information they used to make it? I can still ask those questions. I just don’t know if I’d ask them under my own name. I don’t even know what I think would happen if I did.

I’m starting to do the same thing with my work. I’ll write a line and think about how it would read to someone who wanted a reason to flag it. Then I change it. Sometimes I tell myself it was a better line anyway. Sometimes it is. That makes it harder to tell how much of what I’m making is still my decision.

I wonder what happens to the people who start making things five years from now. By then they might learn to write around these rules the same way I learned to spell. How would they know what they’d have made otherwise?

I almost deleted this. I think I’ll leave it here so I can see whether it still bothers me in a month.

Thank you, Mama,
 for the years before language knew how to hold memory.
 For mornings shaped by routine and care,
 for hands that carried time quietly, without asking to be seen.
 You taught me how to exist before you taught me how to speak,
 how to listen to the world before naming it.
The past lives in small gestures—
 a look, a pause, the way love repeats itself without announcing its name.
 I carry those early rooms inside me,
 where safety was ordinary and devotion was daily.
 I am still becoming what you once protected,
 still walking forward with something ancient holding me from behind.

Tax the rich.
Excess is violence.
No one earns a billion alone.
What is hoarded
was never theirs to keep.
